entries.title: How to use this reference
entries.description: Six parts, numbered clauses, every entry dated and attributed. How the reference is organised, what the numbering means, and where to start depending on why you are here.
sources: ISO/IEC Directives Part 2, rules for the structure of standards

blocks.html:
This is a reference work, not a course. Entries are numbered like clauses in a
standard so you can cite them, link into them, and find your way back.

Six parts, each opening at x.0 with what that part of the function actually produces, then working outward. Every entry carries a review date, a named editor and its sources, because a claim about a framework is worth exactly as much as the thing it cites.

The number before an entry is its clause. 3.2 is the second entry in Part 3; 3.2.1 is the first section inside it. Every section heading is deep-linkable twice — by its slug and by its clause number — so #c3-2-1 and #the-difference-stated-plainly reach the same place.

Clause numbers are stable. If an entry is retired the number is not reused, and if the corpus is renumbered the old anchors redirect.

items.term: You are new to the field
items.html: Read 1.1, then 1.3, then 3.1. That is roughly ninety minutes and gets you to the point where a risk register makes sense.
1.4 for the boundary question, 3.2 for the vocabulary people get wrong, and Part 6 for the rest.
Search, or use the A–Z index. The index uses inverted headwords, so “appetite, risk” and “risk appetite” both land.
Part 2 for the decisions, Part 4 for the obligations, Part 5 for the framework you have been asked for.

blocks.html:
It is not a substitute for the standard. Where an entry describes ISO 27001 or the Trust Services Criteria, it describes them accurately and cites the clause, but the certifiable text is the standard’s and you will need a copy.

It is also not a template library. A few entries link to worked examples; most describe how the artefact behaves and how it fails, which is the part that does not come in a template.

Every entry names an editor. If one is wrong, the “Suggest an edit” link in the header is the fastest route, and corrections are published with an incremented edition rather than quietly patched. The editorial policy sets out how entries are written, reviewed and corrected.

entries.title: What governance, risk and compliance is
entries.description: Governance, risk and compliance is the coordinated set of practices used to direct objectives, understand what could stop them, and prove obligations are met. Definition, the three pillars, and how the frameworks fit.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — Information security management systems, requirements
AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (TSP section 100), 2017, revised 2022

blocks.html: Governance, risk and compliance is the coordinated set of practices an organisation uses to direct what it is trying to achieve, understand what could stop it, and prove it meets the obligations that apply to it.

The three are administered by different people and fail together. Governance sets the appetite that risk measures against; compliance supplies most of the evidence that governance reviews. Run them as three teams with three spreadsheets and the first audit finds the contradictions for you.

The label is younger than the work. Boards have directed, risk functions have measured and compliance officers have evidenced for as long as there have been regulated companies. What changed around 2002 was that the same board committee started receiving all three reports in the same meeting, and noticed they did not agree.

items.html: Who decides, on what authority, and where the decision is recorded — policy set, committee calendar, delegated authority matrix, board reporting.
Identifying what could obstruct the objectives, sizing it, deciding what to do, then watching it — register, appetite statement, treatment plan, issue log.
Knowing which obligations bind you — law, contract, standard — mapping each to a control, and keeping the proof that the control ran.

blocks.html: Each pillar owns artefacts, not opinions. A governance function that cannot produce the minutes recording a decision has not governed it. A risk function whose register has no owners and no dates is a list. A compliance function holding a policy but no evidence the policy was followed has documented an intention.

blocks.name: grc-loop
blocks.caption: FIG. 1 — The GRC loop. Break any edge and the function becomes paperwork: appetite nobody set, controls nobody asked for, evidence nobody reads.

blocks.html:
Read the loop clockwise and it describes a quarter of work. Governance publishes an appetite statement — say, no accepted risk above a residual score of 12 without board sign-off. Risk applies that threshold to the register and produces a treatment plan for everything above it. Compliance runs the controls those treatments name and keeps the evidence. Assurance reports the whole picture back, and governance revises the appetite it set.

Read it anticlockwise and it describes how the function fails. Evidence accumulates with no control mapped to it. Controls run with no risk behind them. Risks are scored against an appetite that was never written down.

The amount of risk an organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its
objectives, stated by governance and used by risk to decide what must be
treated.

columns.html: Most of a GRC analyst’s week is spent moving a risk or a control through a small number of states, and keeping the record of that movement legible to someone who was not there. The interview, the register update, the evidence request, the follow-up when the evidence does not arrive.

columns.caption: FIG. 2 — Risk matrix (5 × 5), the most-used artefact on the job.
columns.note: Outlined cell: a possible / moderate risk — the band where appetite, not arithmetic, decides the answer.

columns.name: register-row
columns.caption: FIG. 3 — A risk register row. The fields that make a score defensible — the same record keyed into any GRC tool.

blocks.html: The matrix is the argument, not the answer. Two people scoring the same incident will land in adjacent cells and both be defensible; what makes the score usable is that the scale is written down, applied the same way twice, and challenged in a forum with minutes. A 5 × 5 grid with no documented criteria behind each band produces numbers that cannot survive a question.

Framework Type Answers the question Output
ISO/IEC 27001 Certification Is the ISMS working? Certificate
NIST CSF 2.0 Framework How mature are we? Profile
SOC 2 Attestation What can we show a customer? Auditor report
COSO ERM Model How does risk reach the board? Risk view

They are not alternatives, and picking between them is usually the wrong question. ISO 27001 and SOC 2 answer different buyers: a certificate travels, an attestation report is read. NIST CSF 2.0 is a language for describing where you are, not a bar to clear — its 2024 revision added a sixth function, Govern, precisely because organisations were maturing controls without anyone owning the decisions behind them. COSO ERM sits above all of it and is about how risk reaches a board at all.

Most organisations of any size end up mapping between at least two of them. That mapping — the crosswalk — is the single most reused artefact in the discipline, because one control almost always satisfies several obligations at once.

items.q: Is GRC a technical job?
items.html:
No, but it is a literate one. You need to read a system diagram and challenge an engineer’s answer; you do not need to configure the system. The daily tools are documents, interviews and evidence.

The failure mode is not being insufficiently technical. It is accepting an answer you did not understand because asking again felt awkward.

items.q: Is GRC the same as cyber security?
items.html:
No. Cyber security is one obligation domain among several — GRC also covers financial reporting, privacy, health and safety, supplier conduct and whatever else the organisation is bound by.

The overlap is large in technology companies, which is why the two are often staffed from the same team, and why “GRC” is frequently used as shorthand for “security compliance”. That shorthand is what makes the boundary confusing. Security engineering builds and operates the control; GRC decides the control is required, tests that it ran, and keeps the proof.

items.q: Which certification should I start with?
items.html:
If you want the vocabulary, ISO/IEC 27001 Lead Implementer or the ISACA CRISC syllabus will both give you it. If you want an employer to recognise the letters, CISA is the most widely asked-for in audit-adjacent roles and does not require a technical background.

Certification is not the gate people entering the field assume it is. A candidate who can walk an interviewer through a risk they assessed end to end — how it was raised, scored, treated, and closed — outperforms one with three certificates and no artefact to describe.

items.q: Can I move into GRC from IT support?
items.html:
It is one of the more common routes in. Service desk work already teaches the two things the role is built on: reading a system you did not build, and writing down what happened in a way someone else can act on.

The gap to close is the evidence habit — knowing what makes a screenshot admissible, why a date matters, and what an auditor will ask for next. That is learnable in months, and considerably faster than teaching a compliance specialist how a directory service works.

entries.title: Terms and definitions
entries.description: The words the rest of the reference assumes. Risk, control, obligation, evidence, assurance and the rest — defined once, in the sense the standards use them.
sources: ISO/IEC 27000:2018 — Information security management systems, overview and vocabulary
IIA, International Professional Practices Framework, Glossary

sections.text: Why the precision earns its keep

blocks.html:
Most arguments inside a GRC function are vocabulary arguments wearing a
disguise. These are the words the rest of the reference uses, in the sense the
standards use them.

Where a term has a precise definition in a standard, that definition is given and cited. Where practice has drifted from the standard — and it has, in several places — the drift is named rather than smoothed over.

items.html: The effect of uncertainty on objectives. Note the direction: a risk is defined against something you are trying to achieve, which is why a register with no objectives behind it drifts into a list of things people dislike.
A risk that has occurred. The distinction is operational: risks are managed on a review cycle, issues are managed to a closure date.
The thing that could cause the event, not the risk itself. “Ransomware” is a threat; “ransomware encrypts the order database and we cannot ship for four days” is a risk.
A measure that modifies risk. Includes process, policy and practice, not only technology — and a control that is not operating is not a control.
A requirement that binds the organisation, from law, regulation, contract or a standard it has committed to. The source is part of the obligation; one with no citation cannot be tested.
A dated record produced by the operation of a control, sufficient for a reviewer who was not present.
A conclusion about whether something works, given by someone with the standing to give it. First party from management, second party from a customer, third party from an independent auditor.
The amount of risk the organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives.
The acceptable variation around a specific objective. Distinct from appetite, and confused with it constantly.
The level before controls are taken into account. Useful mainly for showing what the controls are earning.
The level after existing controls. This is the number appetite is applied to.
What is being done about a risk — accept, mitigate, transfer or avoid.
One named person with the authority to decide. Not a team, not a function, not a role that is currently vacant.
What sits inside the boundary of a certification, an assessment or a register — and by implication what sits outside it, and is therefore unexamined.

blocks.html:
Compliant. Nothing is compliant in the abstract. Something is compliant with a named obligation, at a point in time, on the evidence available. A vendor that says its product is “GDPR compliant” has said nothing testable.

Framework. Used for four different things: a certifiable standard (ISO 27001), a descriptive model (NIST CSF 2.0), an attestation criteria set (SOC 2) and an internal control model (COSO ERM). The difference determines what you can do with the output, which is why it is worth keeping straight.

Maturity. A statement about how consistently a process runs, not about how good it is. A consistently bad process scores well on maturity — which is why a maturity score alone never answers “are we safe”.

The one named person accountable for a risk staying inside appetite, with the
authority to approve its treatment. Distinct from the control owner, who
operates the measure.

blocks.text: Why the precision earns its keep

blocks.html:
An auditor’s first move on a register is to read three risk statements and check they are risks rather than threats or issues. It takes ninety seconds and tells them how much of the rest to trust. The same is true of a control inventory full of aspirations, or an obligation register with no citations.

Getting the words right is not pedantry. It is the cheapest available signal that the function knows what it is doing.

entries.title: The four artefacts every GRC function keeps
entries.description: Every functioning GRC programme keeps the same four records: a policy set, a risk register, a control inventory and an evidence store. What each one is for, and how to tell when one has stopped working.

blocks.html:
Strip a GRC programme of its tooling, its committee names and its reporting
templates, and four records remain. Everything else in the function exists to
create, maintain or read one of them.

The four are a policy set, a risk register, a control inventory and an evidence store. A programme missing one is not necessarily failing, but it will be unable to answer a specific class of question — and the question always arrives.

The written answer to what are we required to do, and who said so. A policy states the rule; a standard states the measurable version of the rule; a procedure states the steps. Three levels, and the confusion between them is the most common documentation problem in a young programme.

The test of a policy set is not whether it exists. It is whether an employee who breaks a rule can be shown the sentence they broke, and whether the person who approved that sentence can be named.

The list of things that could obstruct the objectives, with a score, an owner and a decision attached to each. See 3.1 for how to read one.

A register goes stale in a predictable way: entries stop changing. If nothing in a register has moved a band in two quarters, either the environment is extraordinarily stable or nobody is reviewing it. In practice it is the second.

The list of things you actually do to keep those risks inside appetite, each one mapped to the obligations it satisfies. This is the artefact that makes multiple frameworks affordable — one access review can satisfy an ISO 27001 Annex A control, a SOC 2 criterion and an internal policy at the same time, but only if something records that it does.

An inventory with no mapping column is a to-do list. The mapping is the artefact.

The proof that the controls ran. Screenshots, exports, tickets, signed attestations, meeting minutes — with dates, and with a name attached to whoever produced them.

The quality bar is not “we have a folder”. It is that a stranger can pick a control, pull the evidence for a specific month, and tell from the evidence alone that the control operated. If the evidence needs a colleague to explain it, an auditor will treat it as absent.

A dated record produced by the operation of a control, sufficient for a
reviewer who was not present to conclude the control ran as described.

The four are not independent. A control inventory with no risk register behind it produces controls nobody can justify the cost of. A risk register with no policy set behind it produces scores nobody can challenge, because there is no stated threshold to challenge them against. An evidence store with no inventory is a warehouse.

The order to build them in, when starting from nothing, is register first, then policy, then inventory, then evidence. Starting with policy is the intuitive choice and the slow one: you end up writing rules for risks you have not yet established you carry.
Each of the four is built from a blank page, with a worked example, in GRC Mastery’s foundation track. This entry stays free.

entries.title: GRC vs internal audit vs security engineering
entries.description: GRC designs and operates controls, internal audit independently tests whether they work, and security engineering builds the systems both are talking about. Who owns what, and why the boundary matters.
sources: IIA, International Professional Practices Framework, Standard 1100 (Independence and Objectivity)

blocks.html:
GRC designs and runs the controls. Internal audit independently tests whether
they work. Security engineering builds the systems both are describing. The
three overlap in vocabulary and almost never in accountability.

The confusion is worth resolving early, because the roles look identical from outside — all three read system documentation, all three ask engineers questions, all three write findings — and the difference is entirely about who they answer to.

sides.name: GRC
sides.html:
Designs the control, writes the policy, keeps the register, gathers the
evidence, answers the customer questionnaire. Accountable to management.

sides.name: Internal audit
sides.html:
Samples the same controls without having designed them, forms an opinion,
reports to the audit committee. Independence is the whole job.

blocks.html:
Internal audit’s constraint is the important one. An auditor who helps rewrite the control they will later test has compromised the opinion they exist to give. That is why an internal auditor will point at a gap and decline to close it — not obstruction, but the only position from which the finding is worth anything.

GRC has the opposite mandate. Finding a gap and leaving it open is the failure.

Three-quarters of the confusion is caused by one thing: in organisations under roughly 500 people, the same person often does both. The company has a “compliance manager” who writes the policy, runs the access review, and then signs the attestation saying the access review happened.

That is a self-review, and every framework names it. It is workable while the organisation is small and honest about it; it stops being workable the moment an external party is relying on the attestation.

The impairment created when the party assessing a control is the party that
designed or operated it. Managed by separating the roles, not by declaring
independence.

Security engineering builds and operates the control. GRC establishes that the control is required, defines what “working” means, tests that it ran, and keeps the proof.

In practice the boundary is drawn at the console. If the work involves changing a configuration, it is engineering. If it involves deciding the configuration must be a certain way, or demonstrating to a third party that it was, it is GRC.

The productive relationship between the two is narrower than either expects: GRC should be able to state precisely what evidence it needs and why an obligation demands it, and should not be specifying how the system produces it.

Ask who receives the output. Management receives GRC’s. The audit committee receives internal audit’s. If the answer is “the same person who asked for the work”, it is not audit — whatever the job title says.

entries.title: The three lines model
entries.description: The IIA's 2020 Three Lines Model replaced the older three lines of defence. What each line owns, why "defence" was dropped, and where GRC sits.
sources: IIA, Position Paper: The Three Lines of Defence in Effective Risk Management and Control, 2013

blocks.html:
The three lines model describes how accountability for risk is distributed:
the people doing the work own it, a second group provides expertise and
challenge, and a third gives an independent opinion to the governing body.

The Institute of Internal Auditors published the current version in 2020, replacing a 2013 paper that used the phrase three lines of defence. The rewrite was not cosmetic. “Defence” implied risk was something arriving from outside to be repelled, and implied the lines were sequential barriers. Both readings produced organisations where the first line assumed the second would catch its mistakes.

items.html: The people who deliver the product or service. They own the risks their activity creates and operate the controls inside it. Not a junior line — most control operation happens here.
Specialist functions providing expertise, frameworks, challenge and monitoring. Risk, compliance, and most GRC roles sit here. It supports the first line and reports to management.
Internal audit. Independent assurance to the governing body on the effectiveness of everything the first two lines do. It reports to the audit committee, not to management.

blocks.html: The governing body sits above all three, and management sits between the body and the first two lines. External assurance providers — a certification body, a SOC 2 auditor, a regulator — sit outside the model entirely.

Three things worth knowing if you were taught the older version.

Collaboration replaced separation. The 2013 framing encouraged lines to operate independently of each other. The 2020 model states explicitly that the lines should collaborate, with independence required only for the third.

The lines are roles, not teams. A person can hold first-line and second-line responsibilities in different parts of their job. The model constrains the combination — you cannot independently assure your own work — but does not require three org charts.

Risk is upside as well as downside. The current model frames the lines around achieving objectives, not only avoiding harm.

Second line, in almost every case. GRC provides the frameworks the first line operates within, monitors whether they are being followed, and escalates when they are not.

The common exception: in a small organisation, GRC frequently ends up operating first-line controls too — running the access review rather than checking it ran. That is a resourcing reality rather than a model violation, but it needs to be visible, because it removes the challenge the second line exists to provide.

entries.title: Who does GRC work
entries.description: In a small company one person does all of it. At scale the work splits into risk, compliance, privacy and vendor management. What each seat owns, and who they answer to.
sources: ISACA, State of Cybersecurity, workforce sections, 2025

sections.text: The seats, roughly in the order they appear
The trap in a small company

blocks.html:
In a company of thirty, one person does all of it alongside another job. In a
company of three thousand, the same work is four teams with different reporting
lines. The seats change; the artefacts do not.
The useful way to read an organisation chart here is to ask which of the four artefacts each seat is accountable for, and who receives their output. Titles vary far more than that does.

blocks.text: The seats, roughly in the order they appear

items.html: The first dedicated hire. Runs the register, chases evidence, answers questionnaires, keeps the policy set current. The job is 70% writing things down so somebody else can act on them.
Owns the obligation register and the audit relationship. Appears when there is a second framework, or a first regulator.
Owns the register, the appetite statement and the reporting into committee. Appears when the register outgrows the analyst who started it.
Owns a distinct obligation set with its own regulator and its own artefacts. In the EU the DPO role has statutory independence requirements that make it a poor fit for a general compliance seat.
Owns supplier due diligence and the ongoing monitoring. Usually the first specialisation, because the volume is relentless.
Owns the programme, the budget and the board narrative. Answers for the function’s opinion, not its paperwork.

blocks.html:
Most commonly the CISO, in technology companies where the obligations are security-led. Increasingly the General Counsel where the obligation set is regulatory rather than technical, and occasionally the CFO where it grew out of financial controls.

The reporting line matters less than one thing: whoever it is must not also own the systems being assessed. A GRC function reporting to the engineering leader whose controls it tests is second line in name only.

blocks.text: The trap in a small company

blocks.html:
One person writing the policy, running the access review, and signing the attestation that the access review happened is performing a self-review. Under about a hundred staff this is unavoidable and everybody knows it.

The way to handle it is not to pretend otherwise. Record it in the register as an accepted risk with a named approver, and get a second pair of eyes — a peer, a board member, an external reviewer — on the attestations that leave the building. An auditor who finds the acceptance already written respects it. One who finds it themselves writes a finding.
The first ninety days in a GRC seat, with the artefacts built in order, is the shape of GRC Mastery’s foundation track. This entry stays free.

entries.title: What governance produces
entries.description: Governance is not a meeting. It is four artefacts — a policy set, a committee calendar, a delegated authority matrix and a board pack — and the decisions recorded in them.
sources: COSO, Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

sections.text: What a decision record looks like
Where it goes wrong at small scale

blocks.html:
Governance answers one question in four artefacts: who decided this, on what
authority, and where is it written down.
The test of a governance function is not whether it meets. It is whether, six months later, somebody can find the decision, the person who made it, and the authority they held when they made it.

items.html: The written rules and the standards beneath them. See 2.1 for the three levels and why collapsing them is the standard failure.
Which forums exist, what each one decides, who sits on it, and when it meets. A committee with no terms of reference is a meeting.
Who may approve what, up to what value or severity, without going higher. The artefact that turns “escalate if significant” into something a person can act on at 4pm on a Friday.
What the governing body is told, in what form, on what cycle. See 2.3.

blocks.html:
The distinction is the one COSO and the NIST CSF’s Govern function both turn on. Management runs the organisation. Governance sets the direction management runs in, and holds it to account for the result.

Practically: management decides how to close a gap; governance decides whether the gap is acceptable in the first place, and hears about it either way. When the same forum does both, the challenge disappears — the group approving the plan is the group that wrote it.

blocks.text: What a decision record looks like

blocks.html:
The minimum that survives a year: the question put, the options considered, the decision, the person or forum that made it, the date, and the authority relied on. Six lines.

Most governance failures found in audit are not bad decisions. They are good decisions with no record of who made them, discovered at the moment somebody needs to know whether they were entitled to.

The specific power a role holds to decide without escalating, stated with its
limit. An authority with no limit is not delegated — it is assumed.

blocks.text: Where it goes wrong at small scale

blocks.html:
A twenty-person company does not need four committees. It needs the four artefacts to exist in some form, and one of them is usually a shared document rather than a governance platform.

The failure at this size is not absent governance; it is undocumented governance. The founders genuinely do decide things, consistently, on defensible grounds — and none of it is written down, so the first customer security review finds a company that cannot show it governs anything.

entries.title: Policy, standard, procedure — the document hierarchy
entries.description: A policy states the rule, a standard states the measurable version, a procedure states the steps. Getting the three levels wrong is the most common documentation failure in a young GRC programme.

blocks.html: Three levels, and each answers a different question. The policy says what is required. The standard says how much is enough. The procedure says how to do it.

Collapsing them is the standard failure. An organisation writes one forty-page “Information Security Policy” containing password lengths and step-by-step joiner instructions, then discovers it must go back to the board every time a tool changes.

Level Answers Changes Approved by
Policy What is required, and why Rarely — annually at most Board or delegated committee
Standard How much is enough, measurably When the threat or tooling moves Function head
Procedure How the work is done, step by step Whenever the tool changes Process owner

The approval column is the reason the split exists. Different levels change at different speeds and warrant different levels of scrutiny; binding them into one document forces the slowest approval path onto the fastest-moving content.

Policy: access to systems holding customer data is granted on the principle of least privilege and reviewed at defined intervals.

Standard: privileged access is reviewed quarterly; standard access semi-annually; reviews are completed within 15 working days of issue.

Procedure: export the entitlement report from the identity provider, filter to the in-scope groups, distribute to the named owners, track responses in the review tracker, revoke on instruction, attach the completed tracker to the control record.

Note what moves where. Replace the identity provider and only the procedure changes. Tighten the cadence to monthly and only the standard changes. The policy is untouched by either.

The principle that an identity holds only the access required for its current
duties, for only as long as those duties last.

A policy that names a product is a standard. A standard with no number in it is a policy. A procedure that requires judgement to follow is a standard pretending.

One more, useful when reviewing someone else’s document set: pick any rule and ask who approved it and when. If nobody can answer for a rule the organisation is enforcing against employees, the hierarchy has failed regardless of how many levels it has on paper.

entries.title: Committees and delegated authority
entries.description: A committee with no terms of reference is a meeting, and an authority with no limit is not delegated. How to write both so a decision at 4pm on a Friday does not need an escalation.
sources: COSO, Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

sections.text: Terms of reference, in six lines
The escalation trigger that actually works
How many forums a company actually needs

blocks.html:
A committee exists to make a class of decision that no individual should make
alone. If you cannot name that class, you have scheduled a meeting.
Two artefacts do this work: terms of reference, which say what a forum decides, and a delegated authority matrix, which says what everybody else may decide without it.

blocks.text: Terms of reference, in six lines

blocks.html:
Purpose — the class of decision this forum owns. Membership — by role, with a quorum. Cadence. Inputs — what must be tabled, by whom, how far in advance. Outputs — minutes, decisions, actions with owners and dates. Escalation — what this forum sends upward, and on what trigger.

Anything longer is usually a description of the organisation rather than a mandate. Anything shorter cannot settle an argument about whether a decision was in scope.
One row per decision type, one column per level, and a limit in every cell.

The badly written version is the common one, and it fails in a specific way: it cannot be applied by the person holding it. “Escalate if significant” means the holder must guess at the threshold, and every guess is defensible afterwards, which means nothing is.

blocks.text: The escalation trigger that actually works

blocks.html:
Tie it to the appetite statement. If governance has published no accepted risk above a residual score of 12 without board sign-off, the matrix inherits that number and the trigger is arithmetic rather than judgement.

Where appetite is qualitative, the trigger has to be categorical instead — any risk touching customer funds, any obligation with a regulatory penalty attached. Either works. What does not work is a trigger that requires the person pulling it to already know the answer.

The minimum attendance for a forum’s decisions to stand. Worth setting low
enough that the committee can actually meet, and specific enough that three
people from the same team cannot constitute it.

blocks.text: How many forums a company actually needs

blocks.html:
One, until it does not. A single risk and compliance forum, meeting quarterly, with the CEO or COO in the chair, covers most organisations under two hundred people and produces a real minute trail.

Split it when the agenda stops fitting — usually when privacy or a regulator arrives with its own reporting obligations. Splitting earlier produces forums that meet without a decision to make, which is how a governance calendar starts being ignored.

entries.title: Board reporting
entries.description: A board pack answers three questions in one page: what changed, what is outside appetite, and what we need from you. Everything else is an appendix.
sources: COSO, Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

blocks.html:
A board has perhaps twelve minutes for your item. The pack that works answers
three questions in that time: what changed, what sits outside appetite, and
what you need the board to decide.
Everything else — the register extract, the control coverage, the audit timetable — belongs in an annex nobody is expected to read in the room, and everybody can read afterwards.

What changed. Since the last meeting, in the language of the business. Two new risks above appetite because the payments integration went live; one closed because the supplier was replaced. Not a delta count.

What is outside appetite. The specific entries, their owners, the treatment and the date. This is the only part of the pack that requires a decision, and it should be visually obvious which items they are.

What you need. A decision, a budget, or an acknowledgement. Say which. A pack that asks for nothing trains the board to skim it.

A four-colour grid with dots on it is the most requested and least useful board artefact in the discipline. It shows position without showing movement, compresses away the ownership, and invites an argument about whether something is amber or red rather than about what to do.

If the board wants one, give them one — and put the movement beside it. An arrow per entry showing where it was last quarter turns the same picture into a narrative, which is what a board is actually assembling.

The papers issued in advance of a governing-body meeting. Issued late, it is a
document read in the room; issued a week ahead, it is a document the board has
questions about.

Three questions come up in almost every session, and the pack is stronger if it pre-empts them.

Is this getting better or worse? Answered by trend, not by level.

What would you do with more money? Answered by the treatments currently deferred, with what deferring them costs.

What are we not seeing? Answered honestly by naming the parts of the estate outside scope, which is uncomfortable and builds more credit than anything else in the pack.

Quarterly, with an out-of-cycle path for anything material. Monthly reporting to a board produces packs nobody reads and a function that spends its time reporting rather than working; annual reporting produces surprises.

The out-of-cycle path matters more than the cadence. A board that learns about a significant incident from the quarterly pack six weeks later will not trust the quarterly pack again.

entries.title: What the risk function produces
entries.description: A register, an appetite statement, a treatment plan and an issue log. What each is for, how they connect, and the order to build them in.
keywords: what does a risk function do
sources: ISO/IEC 27005:2022 — Guidance on managing information security risks

sections.text: What good looks like after a year

blocks.html:
The risk function produces four things: a register of what could go wrong, a
statement of how much of it is acceptable, a plan for the rest, and a log of
what has already happened.
ISO 31000 describes the process — identify, analyse, evaluate, treat, monitor, communicate — but the artefacts are what other people actually consume, and each one fails in a recognisable way.

items.html: What could obstruct the objectives, sized, owned and decided. See 3.1. Fails by going stale.
How much risk is acceptable, by category, with a threshold. See 3.2. Fails by being too abstract to apply.
What is being done about everything above the threshold, with owners and dates. See 3.3. Fails by filling with “monitor”.
Risks that have occurred, managed to closure rather than on a cycle. Fails by being kept separately from the register, so nobody notices the risk was known.

blocks.html:
Governance publishes the appetite. Risk scores the register against it. Anything above the threshold gets a treatment with an owner and a date; anything below is monitored on its review cycle. When a risk occurs it moves to the issue log, keeps its history, and is reviewed on closure to ask whether the score was wrong.

Break the last link and the function loses the only feedback it gets. A register that never learns from its own issues is a forecast nobody scores.

Register first, even a rough one. Twenty entries written badly beat an empty template, because the argument about the scale is easier to have with real entries in front of it.

Appetite second, once there is something to apply it to. Writing appetite first produces a statement calibrated against nothing.

Treatment third. Issue log last, or rather immediately — you will need it the first week, and it is a table.

The written basis for judging significance: the likelihood and impact scales,
the bands, and what each band means. Undocumented criteria produce scores that
cannot be defended or repeated.

blocks.text: What good looks like after a year

blocks.html:
Entries move. Ownership is individual. The top ten are genuinely the top ten rather than the ten written first. Somebody outside the function can pick an entry and follow it from raise to treatment to closure without asking a question.

That last test is the one that matters, and the one most programmes fail.

entries.title: Reading a risk register for the first time
entries.description: A risk register is a list of what could obstruct the objectives, with a score, an owner and a decision on each. The columns that matter, and the four signs a register has stopped being maintained.
sources: ISO/IEC 27005:2022 — Guidance on managing information security risks
COSO, Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

sections.text: The scoring, and what it is for
Four signs a register has stopped working
What to do when handed one cold

blocks.html:
A risk register is the list of things that could stop the organisation
achieving what it set out to do, each with a size, a named owner, and a
decision about what happens next.
It is the most-read artefact in the discipline and the most frequently abandoned. Both facts have the same cause: a register is cheap to start and expensive to keep honest.

items.html: A cause, an event and a consequence in one sentence. “Supplier X fails, our checkout is unavailable, we lose transactions and breach the SLA.” Not a topic — “supply chain” is not a risk.
How large it would be with no controls in place. Argued over more than it deserves; useful mainly for showing how much the controls are earning.
What is currently in place, mapped to the control inventory rather than described freehand.
The size after those controls. This is the number the appetite is applied to.
One named person who can authorise the treatment. Not a team, not a function.
Accept, mitigate, transfer or avoid — with a date and a target score if it is anything but accept.
When somebody last looked, and when they will look next.

blocks.html: Registers commonly carry more columns than this. They rarely carry fewer and remain usable.

blocks.text: The scoring, and what it is for

blocks.html:
Likelihood times impact, on whatever scale the organisation has documented — usually 5 × 5, giving scores from 1 to 25. See 1.1 for the matrix itself.

Precision is not the goal. Two competent assessors will land in adjacent cells, and that is fine. What matters is that the bands are defined in writing, that a score can be traced to the criteria that produced it, and that the same criteria were applied last quarter. A register whose scale lives in one person’s head produces numbers that evaporate when they leave.

The level of risk remaining after existing controls are taken into account. The
number appetite is tested against.

blocks.text: Four signs a register has stopped working

blocks.html:
Nothing has moved in two quarters. Scores that never change mean nobody is reassessing them. Real registers churn.

Every owner is a team. “Owned by: Engineering” means owned by nobody. When the treatment slips, there is no one to ask.

The treatment column reads “monitor”. Monitoring is not a treatment; it is the absence of one, written to avoid the accept decision that someone would have to sign.

Closed risks disappear. A risk that was accepted and later closed should still be visible with its history. A register that only shows what is open cannot answer “did we know about this?”, which is the question asked after an incident.

blocks.text: What to do when handed one cold

blocks.html: Sort by residual score descending. Read the top ten statements and check each is a sentence with a consequence in it. Look at the review dates. Then find the appetite statement and check the top ten are actually above it — if they are not, either the appetite is set too high to be meaningful, or the register is only recording what was comfortable to write down.
Building a register from a blank sheet, and defending the scores in a committee, is the first module of GRC Mastery’s foundation track. This entry stays free.

entries.title: Risk appetite vs risk tolerance
entries.description: Appetite is how much risk the organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives. Tolerance is the acceptable variation around a specific objective. One is a stance, the other is a boundary.
sources: COSO, Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

blocks.html: Appetite is the amount of risk an organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives. Tolerance is the acceptable variation around a particular objective. Appetite is a stance; tolerance is a boundary on a number.

The two are used interchangeably in conversation and mean different things in every framework that defines them. The distinction matters at exactly one moment: when someone has to decide whether a specific risk gets treated or accepted.

Appetite is set once a year, by the board, and covers a category. We accept moderate operational risk to enter new markets quickly; we accept no risk that would compromise customer funds. It is directional and mostly qualitative.

Tolerance is the numeric edge on a specific objective. Availability must not fall below 99.5% in any calendar month. Cross it and something specific happens — an escalation, a treatment, a board paper.

Appetite tells you which risks you are in the business of taking. Tolerance tells you when a particular one has gone too far.

Most published appetite statements cannot be applied to a decision, which is the only test that matters. The three ways they fail:

Too abstract to test. “We have a low appetite for cyber risk” cannot resolve a specific question. Against what score, in what category, approved by whom?

No threshold. An appetite with no number attached cannot tell you whether the risk in front of you is inside it. The usable form names a residual score — no accepted risk above 12 without board sign-off — even when the category framing stays qualitative.

Uniform across categories. An organisation genuinely has different appetites for different things. A single statement covering all risk is either so permissive it permits everything or so restrictive it is ignored.

The maximum risk the organisation could absorb before it becomes unable to
operate. Appetite is set below capacity; the gap is deliberate.

The risk function scores an entry, produces a residual figure, and compares it against the appetite threshold for that category. Above it, the entry needs a treatment plan or a documented acceptance at the right level of authority. Below it, the entry is monitored on its review cycle.

Tolerance operates in a different loop, usually automated: a metric crosses a line, someone is notified, an issue is raised. It is the operational tripwire; appetite is the annual stance the tripwire was placed to protect.

Get the two the wrong way round — an appetite reviewed monthly, a tolerance argued about annually — and the function spends its time on the wrong meeting.

entries.title: Risk treatment options
entries.description: Four options and nothing else — accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid. What each commits you to, what evidence each needs, and which one "monitor" is really hiding.

sections.text: Why "monitor" is not on the list
What each treatment has to evidence
Sequencing when everything is above appetite

blocks.html:
There are four treatments and no others. Accept it, reduce it, move it to
somebody else, or stop doing the thing that creates it.

Every entry above appetite carries one of them, with an owner and a date. The value of the closed list is that it forces a decision: a risk with no treatment selected has not been decided about, however much has been written under it.

items.html: Take the risk as it stands. Requires an approval at the right level of authority, recorded with a date and a review point. Acceptance is a decision, not the absence of one.
Add or strengthen a control so the residual score falls. Requires a target score, a control that will exist, an owner and a date. Most treatments are this.

Move the financial consequence elsewhere — insurance, a contractual indemnity, an outsourced service. Note what does not transfer: the regulatory obligation and the reputational consequence almost never do.
Stop the activity. Rare, and usually the right answer exactly once, when the activity was never worth its risk.

blocks.text: Why "monitor" is not on the list

blocks.html:
It is the most common entry in a treatment column and it is the absence of a treatment, written to avoid the acceptance decision somebody would have to sign.

Everything is monitored — that is what the review cycle is. Writing “monitor” says the risk is being accepted without anybody putting their name to the acceptance, which is precisely the situation the register exists to prevent.

If the answer is genuinely accept, write accept, and get it approved. It is a respectable answer and auditors treat it as one.

blocks.text: What each treatment has to evidence

rows.a: Approval at the right authority, dated
Target score, named control, owner, date
The contract or policy, and what it excludes
rows.b: Cover still in force, limits still adequate

rows.a: Decision record, and confirmation the activity stopped

blocks.html: The right-hand column is the one programmes skip. A mitigation approved eighteen months ago, whose control was never built, still shows a reduced residual score in most registers — which makes the register actively misleading rather than merely stale.

The score a mitigation is expected to reach, stated when the treatment is
chosen. Without it there is no test for whether the treatment worked.

blocks.text: Sequencing when everything is above appetite

blocks.html:
A new programme frequently finds twenty entries above the threshold and capacity for four. The instinct is to lower the appetite until the list fits, which destroys the artefact.

The honest move is to treat four, accept the rest explicitly with a named approver and a shorter review cycle, and put the acceptance list in front of governance. That converts a resourcing problem into a decision the organisation has actually made, which is both defensible in audit and considerably more likely to release budget.

entries.title: Risk capacity, and the gap below it
entries.description: Capacity is the most risk the organisation could absorb before it stops functioning. Appetite is set below it deliberately, and the gap is the point.
sources: COSO, Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

sections.text: The gap, and why it is deliberate

blocks.html:
Risk capacity is the maximum an organisation could absorb before it becomes
unable to operate. Appetite is set below it on purpose, and the distance between
them is the margin the business is choosing to keep.

Three terms sit on one line and are routinely collapsed into each other: capacity, appetite, tolerance. Capacity is a fact about the balance sheet and the licence. Appetite is a choice. Tolerance is a limit on a specific number.

Capacity is not a score. It is expressed in whatever would actually run out.

Money. The loss that would breach a covenant, exhaust the cash runway, or require an emergency raise.

Time. The outage after which contracted customers may terminate, which is usually written in your own service agreements and rarely read by the risk function.

Licence. The regulatory finding that would suspend an authorisation. Binary, and in regulated sectors it is the binding constraint regardless of the money.

An organisation that has never expressed capacity in at least one of these has no basis for saying its appetite is set conservatively — it has nothing to be conservative relative to.

blocks.text: The gap, and why it is deliberate

blocks.html:
Appetite below capacity leaves room for the risks you did not identify. That is its whole function. A programme that sets appetite at capacity is claiming its register is complete, which no register is.

How wide the gap should be is a board judgement, not a formula. What is reasonable to expect is that the board has been shown both numbers on the same page at least once, and has said the gap is the one it wants.

Applying a plausible severe scenario to the register and asking whether the
combined effect stays inside capacity. The only routine way to find out whether
the gap is real.

Rarely in daily work, which is why it goes missing. It matters at exactly three moments: setting appetite, approving a large acceptance, and after an incident, when somebody asks how close that came.

The third is when a function that has never articulated capacity discovers it cannot answer the only question the board wants answered.

entries.title: What compliance produces
entries.description: An obligation register, a control inventory mapped to it, an evidence store and an audit response. The four artefacts, and the mapping that makes several frameworks affordable at once.

sections.text: Compliance is not the same as being safe

blocks.html:
Compliance knows which obligations bind the organisation, maps each one to a
control, and keeps the proof that the control ran. Three verbs, four artefacts.

The distinguishing artefact is the mapping. Without it a company running two frameworks does the same work twice and produces two control inventories that disagree — which is worse than either alone, because now nobody knows which one an auditor will be shown.

items.html: Every requirement that binds you, with its source cited — the law, the clause, the contract, the standard. An obligation with no citation cannot be tested and will not survive challenge.
What you actually do, each control mapped to the obligations it satisfies. See 4.1.
The dated proof that each control operated, retrievable by control and by period. See 4.2.
The process for receiving a request, producing the evidence, and managing what comes back. See 4.3.

blocks.html:
Four sources, and programmes routinely forget the third and fourth.

Law and regulation, which is the one everybody starts with. Contracts — customer agreements with security schedules, supplier terms, insurance conditions. Standards the organisation has voluntarily committed to, which bind in practice once a certificate is on the website. And internal policy, which binds because you wrote it down and told people to follow it.

The contractual set is usually the largest and the least catalogued. A company with two hundred customer contracts has agreed to a lot of specific things and frequently cannot list them.

One quarterly access review can satisfy an ISO 27001 Annex A control, a SOC 2 criterion, a customer contractual clause and an internal policy — with the same evidence, produced once.

That only happens if something records the relationship. An inventory with no mapping column is a to-do list; the mapping is what turns a control programme into a compliance programme.

A requirement binding the organisation, from law, contract, standard or its own
policy, recorded with the source that creates it.

blocks.text: Compliance is not the same as being safe

blocks.html:
Worth stating plainly, because the conflation causes real harm in both directions. A compliant organisation has met a defined set of obligations. Those obligations were written by somebody else, against a general case, at a point in the past.

They are a floor. The risk function exists to find what the floor does not cover, and a compliance programme that has quietly replaced the risk register with a control checklist has removed the only part of the function that was looking at your specific situation.

sections.text: Building it without losing a month

blocks.html:
A mapping records which controls satisfy which obligations. It is the artefact
that makes a second framework cost a fraction of the first, and the one most
programmes build last and regret.

The relationship is many-to-many in both directions. One control commonly satisfies six obligations; one obligation commonly needs three controls. Any model that assumes otherwise produces a mapping that has to be rebuilt.

items.html: Stable, and not the framework’s. Borrow ISO’s A.5.15 as your control ID and you will renumber the whole inventory when you add SOC 2.
What is done, in the present tense, specific enough to test. “Access is reviewed” is not testable; “privileged access to production is reviewed quarterly by the system owner” is.
The named person who operates it. Distinct from the risk owner.
How often it runs, which determines how many evidence instances an auditor will expect.
The list, with citations. This is the mapping.
What the control produces, and where it lands.

blocks.text: Building it without losing a month

blocks.html:
Start from the controls, not the frameworks. List what the organisation already does — the access review, the change approval, the backup test, the onboarding checklist — and write each as a testable statement with an owner.

Then take the framework you have been asked for and walk its requirements against that list. Three things fall out: controls that map cleanly, controls you have that nothing requires, and requirements nothing covers. The third list is your gap analysis, and it arrives as a by-product rather than as a separate six-week exercise.

Adding the second framework then takes days rather than months, because you are walking a second requirement set against an inventory that already exists.

Mapping to the framework’s structure. If your inventory is organised as Annex A, then SOC 2 has to be bolted on sideways, and NIST CSF cannot be expressed at all. Organise by what you do; map outward.

One-to-one mapping. Filling every requirement with exactly one control produces controls invented to satisfy a requirement rather than to manage a risk — and an inventory full of controls nobody runs. Some requirements are satisfied by three controls; some by a documented justification for exclusion.

A different control accepted as meeting an obligation the prescribed control
would have met, with a documented rationale. Legitimate, and audited harder than
the original.

The mapping decays at every framework revision and every reorganisation. Two habits keep it alive: review it when a control owner changes rather than annually, and treat a new customer contract clause as an obligation-register event rather than a legal one.

The second is the one that catches programmes out. A security schedule agreed by the sales team in March is an obligation from March, and the first anybody in compliance hears of it is usually the audit.

entries.title: Evidence that holds up in audit
entries.description: Audit-grade evidence is dated, attributable, complete for the period, and intelligible to someone who was not there. The four properties, and the screenshot habits that fail all of them.
sources: IIA, International Professional Practices Framework, Standard 2310 (Identifying Information)

sections.text: What to keep, and for how long

blocks.html:
Evidence is a dated record produced by the operation of a control, sufficient
for a reviewer who was not present to conclude that the control ran as
described. Everything else is documentation.
The gap between “we do this” and “we can show we did this” is where most first audits are lost, and it is almost never because the control was not running.

items.html: The record shows when the control ran, in a way the system produced rather than a person typed. A screenshot with no visible timestamp establishes nothing about when.
It is clear who performed the action and who reviewed it. A shared account performing a control makes attribution impossible and usually makes the control itself a finding.
An auditor testing a quarterly control over a year expects four instances, not the best one. Evidence for three of four quarters is a gap, not a near miss.
A stranger can tell from the artefact what happened. If it needs a colleague to narrate it, the auditor records it as unsupported.

blocks.html: Completeness is the one that fails most often, and it fails quietly — a programme collects excellent evidence for the months someone remembered.

Screenshots are accepted evidence and are also the weakest common form. Cropped to hide the URL, taken after the fact, showing a filtered view with the filter out of frame, undated because the clock was outside the capture area.

Where a system can export, export. A CSV of the entitlement review with the generation timestamp in it beats twelve screenshots, is faster to produce, and cannot be accused of selection.

Where only a screenshot is possible, capture the whole window — URL bar, system clock, the account signed in, and the filter state.

blocks.text: What to keep, and for how long

blocks.html: Keep the artefact, the control it evidences, and the period it covers, linked so that any one of the three retrieves the others. The retention floor is the audit period plus one year, because the following year’s audit will sample the prior period to test consistency. Contracts and regulations frequently demand longer.

Testing a subset of a control’s instances to conclude on the whole population.
The auditor selects the sample, which is why evidence must be complete rather
than representative.

Collect at the point of operation, not at the point of request. A control that files its own evidence — the review tool exporting on completion, the ticket closing with the export attached — takes minutes once and survives audit. Evidence gathered in the four weeks before fieldwork takes the whole four weeks and still has holes in it.

sections.text: What to do when the evidence is not there
Handling a finding you disagree with
The habit that makes audits boring

blocks.html:
An audit is a sampling exercise. The auditor selects which instances of a
control they want to see, you produce them, and the quality of the programme
shows in how few surprises that produces.
The single most useful thing to understand going in: you do not choose the sample. A programme that has collected its best evidence rather than all of it discovers this in week one of fieldwork.

Planning. Scope, period, control list, timetable. This is the moment to correct a misunderstanding about scope, and the last cheap moment to do it.

Fieldwork. Requests arrive, usually in batches, usually with a turnaround of a few days each. Someone must own the queue. Two to four weeks for a first external audit.

Findings. Draft findings come with a right of reply. Read the wording closely — the difference between “the control was not operating” and “evidence of operation was not retained” is large and often negotiable on fact.

Response and closure. Management response, remediation plan, dates. Then either closure or carry-forward to the next cycle.

blocks.text: What to do when the evidence is not there

blocks.html:
Say so, immediately, in writing.

The instinct is to reconstruct — regenerate the report today and present it as though it were produced in March. Auditors are extremely good at spotting this, it converts a control finding into an integrity finding, and integrity findings follow a programme for years.

The right move is to state that the instance is missing, say why, say what has changed so the next period is complete, and let it be a finding. A programme that self-reports a gap is treated very differently from one caught concealing the same gap.

blocks.text: Handling a finding you disagree with

blocks.html:
Two kinds of disagreement, handled differently.

Factual — the auditor has the control wrong, or has tested the wrong system. Answer with evidence, not argument, and expect it to be resolved.

Judgement — you both agree what happened and disagree about severity. This is what the management response is for. Say what you accept, say what you dispute and why, and record it. You will not usually win, and the record still matters: it is the thing you point at next year when the same finding is raised against a control you deliberately chose not to change.

Testing a subset of a control’s instances to conclude on the whole population.
Because the auditor selects the sample, evidence must be complete rather than
representative.

blocks.text: The habit that makes audits boring

blocks.html:
Run one internally, first, on a handful of controls, with someone who did not operate them pulling the evidence. It takes two days, finds most of what the real audit would find, and moves the discovery from fieldwork to a quiet Tuesday.

Programmes that do this describe audits as administrative. Programmes that do not describe them as the worst month of the year, and both are accurate.

entries.title: How to read a framework
entries.description: Four kinds of document get called a framework, and they answer different questions. Which one you are holding determines what you can do with the output.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — Information security management systems, requirements
COSO, Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

sections.text: The two questions that sort them
What overlaps and what does not

blocks.html:
Four different kinds of document are called frameworks, and they are not
alternatives. Which kind you are holding decides what its output is worth to
whoever asked for it.
The question “which framework should we do” is nearly always answered by who is asking and what they will accept, not by the merits of the documents.

items.html: Specifies requirements a management system must meet. An accredited body audits against it and issues a certificate. ISO/IEC 27001, ISO 9001, ISO 22301.
Criteria a practitioner tests your described controls against, producing a report rather than a certificate. SOC 2 against the Trust Services Criteria.
A vocabulary and structure for describing where you are. Not a bar to clear, and nothing certifies against it. NIST CSF 2.0, with its six functions.
A model of how control and risk should reach a governing body. Used to design a programme, not to test one. COSO ERM, the IIA’s Three Lines Model.

blocks.text: The two questions that sort them

blocks.html:
What does it produce? A certificate travels and can be published. A report is read, usually under NDA, and says considerably more. A profile or a maturity score says where you are and binds you to nothing. A model produces a design.

Who audits it? An accredited certification body, a licensed practitioner, yourself, or nobody. This is what determines whether the output means anything to a third party — a self-assessed anything is worth exactly the trust already placed in you.

Three things to find before anything else.

The scope clause. Every certifiable standard has one, and it is where the real negotiation happens. A certificate covering one product line is not a certificate covering the company, and the scope statement is printed on it.

The shall/should boundary. In a standard, “shall” is a requirement and “should” is a recommendation. Auditors test the first and ask about the second. Reading a standard without noticing which is which produces a programme that gold-plates recommendations and misses requirements.

The annex’s status. ISO 27001’s Annex A is a reference control set you justify including or excluding, not a checklist you complete. Treating it as mandatory is the single most expensive misreading in the discipline.

The oversight of the certification bodies themselves, by a national
accreditation body. An unaccredited certificate is a document a company bought.

blocks.text: What overlaps and what does not

blocks.html:
The controls overlap heavily — access, change, vulnerabilities, incidents, vendors, backups. The shells do not: ISO wants a management system with internal audit and management review; SOC 2 wants a system description and the auditor’s own testing; NIST CSF wants neither and gives you a profile.

Budget for one control programme and as many reporting shells as you have buyers. See 5.2 for the artefact that makes that affordable.

entries.title: ISO 27001 vs SOC 2
entries.description: ISO 27001 certifies a management system and produces a certificate. SOC 2 is an attestation over control operation and produces a report. Which one your buyer is actually asking for.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — Information security management systems, requirements
AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (TSP section 100), 2017, revised 2022

sections.text: The overlap, and why it pays

blocks.html:
ISO/IEC 27001 certifies that a management system exists and works, and produces
a certificate. SOC 2 attests that specific controls operated over a period, and
produces a report someone reads. They answer different questions for different
buyers.
The question “which should we do first” is nearly always settled by who is asking for it, not by the merits of either standard.

sides.name: ISO/IEC 27001
sides.html:
An accredited body audits your ISMS against the standard and issues a
certificate you can publish. Annex A supplies a reference control set you
justify including or excluding.

sides.name: SOC 2
sides.html:
A licensed CPA firm tests the controls you describe against the Trust Services
Criteria and writes a report, usually shared under NDA. No fixed control list —
you describe your own, then prove them.

rows.b: Type I point in time; Type II a period

blocks.html: The fixed-control-list row is the structural difference and the one that surprises people. ISO 27001 hands you a reference set of controls in Annex A and asks you to justify inclusions and exclusions in a Statement of Applicability. SOC 2 hands you criteria and asks you to describe the controls you have chosen to meet them. One is a checklist you argue with; the other is an essay you must then prove.

The document recording which Annex A controls apply, which do not, and the
justification for each decision. Required by ISO/IEC 27001 clause 6.1.3 d).

A distinction only SOC 2 has, and the one most often got wrong in sales conversations.

Type I says the controls were suitably designed at a point in time. It is a snapshot, achievable quickly, and a sophisticated buyer will note that it proves nothing about operation.

Type II says the controls operated effectively across a period — commonly three to twelve months. This is what enterprise procurement means when it says “SOC 2”. A first Type II usually covers a shorter window, then extends to twelve months on the next cycle.

blocks.text: The overlap, and why it pays

blocks.html:
The control sets overlap substantially. Access review, change management, vulnerability management, incident response, vendor management and backup do work for both, with the same evidence.

What does not transfer is the shell around them. ISO 27001 requires management system machinery — scope, policy, risk assessment methodology, internal audit, management review, corrective action — that SOC 2 has no equivalent of. SOC 2 requires a system description and a control matrix in a specific form, plus an auditor’s own testing, which ISO does not.

Budget for one control programme and two reporting shells. Organisations that budget for two programmes spend roughly twice what they need to and produce two inconsistent control inventories, which is worse than the cost.

If your buyers are North American technology companies, they will ask for SOC 2 and many will not recognise an ISO certificate. If they are European, or enterprise procurement anywhere, they will ask for ISO 27001. If they are both, do the control work once and sequence the reporting — SOC 2 Type I first for speed, ISO 27001 next for reach, SOC 2 Type II on the following cycle.
The crosswalk between Annex A and the Trust Services Criteria is built line by line in GRC Mastery’s frameworks track. This entry stays free.

entries.title: Building a control crosswalk
entries.description: A crosswalk maps one framework's requirements onto another through your own controls. How to build one that survives a revision, and why mapping framework-to-framework directly is the wrong shape.

sections.text: Hub and spoke, not point to point
What a revision does to it

blocks.html:
A crosswalk lets one control answer several frameworks at once. Built correctly
it is the reason a second certification costs a fraction of the first; built
incorrectly it is a spreadsheet that has to be thrown away at the next revision.
The critical decision is the shape. Almost every published crosswalk maps framework A directly to framework B, and almost every useful internal one maps both through your own control inventory.

blocks.text: Hub and spoke, not point to point

blocks.html:
Direct mapping produces one artefact per pair. Three frameworks means three mappings; four means six. Each is maintained separately and they drift.

Mapping through your controls means one artefact. Each control lists the requirements it satisfies across every framework you carry. Adding a fourth framework adds one column, not three documents.
The last row is where the confusion comes from. Vendors publish framework-to-framework crosswalks because they are marketable. They are a useful starting reference and a poor operating artefact.

Take the control inventory from 4.1. For each framework, walk its requirements and record against each control the requirements it satisfies. Three outputs, as always: mapped, unmapped requirements, and controls nothing requires.

Two rules keep it honest. A mapping is a claim that this control, as written, satisfies that requirement — if it only partly does, record it as partial and name the gap, because a partial mapping recorded as full is exactly what fieldwork finds. And every mapping cites the requirement identifier, not its paraphrase, so a revision can be diffed.

blocks.text: What a revision does to it

blocks.html:
ISO 27001 moved from 114 Annex A controls in 2013 to 93 in 2022, restructured into four themes. Organisations with a hub-and-spoke crosswalk re-mapped one column. Organisations with three pairwise mappings rebuilt all of them.

Assume a revision every three to five years per framework and build for it.

A control that satisfies part of a requirement, recorded with what it does not
cover. The honest form, and the one that stops a gap being discovered during
fieldwork.

For a company adding SOC 2 to an existing ISO 27001 programme, the control work is largely done and the crosswalk shows exactly which parts. What remains is the system description, the auditor’s testing, and the handful of criteria ISO does not reach.

The saving is not the certificate. It is that the second audit examines a programme that already runs, rather than a programme assembled to be examined.

entries.title: The statement of applicability
entries.description: The SoA records which ISO 27001 Annex A controls apply, which do not, and why — a decision record, not an inventory. Required by clause 6.1.3 d).

sections.text: How it relates to your other artefacts

blocks.html:
The statement of applicability records which Annex A controls apply to your
ISMS, which do not, and the justification for each decision. ISO/IEC 27001
clause 6.1.3 d) requires it, and the auditor reads it before anything else.

It is a decision record, not a control inventory. That distinction is where most first attempts go wrong: a document listing 93 controls with “implemented” beside each says nothing about why any of them applies to you.

items.html: The Annex A identifier, from the 2022 revision’s 93 controls across four themes — organisational, people, physical, technological.
Yes or no. Not “partially” — a control either applies to your scope or it does not.
Why. For an inclusion this is usually the risk it treats or the obligation it meets; for an exclusion it is why the scope does not reach it.
Whether it is in place, and where the detail lives — a pointer to your own control inventory rather than a description.

blocks.html: The justification column is the one that gets skimmed and the one that is read hardest. “Applicable — best practice” is not a justification. “Applicable — treats R-014, remote access to production” is.

Excluding a control is legitimate and expected. A company with no physical premises excludes several physical controls; a company that writes no software excludes secure development controls.

What is not legitimate is excluding a control because it is inconvenient. The justification is tested, and the obvious tell is an exclusion that contradicts the scope statement — no development controls, in a scope covering a product the company builds.

Where an exclusion is genuine, the phrasing that survives is the one that ties back to scope rather than to circumstance: not “we do not currently do this”, but “this activity is outside the ISMS scope defined in clause 4.3”.

blocks.text: How it relates to your other artefacts

blocks.html:
The SoA is the bridge between the risk assessment and the control inventory. The risk assessment says what needs treating; the SoA says which Annex A controls are in play as a result; the inventory says what you actually do and who owns it.

Keeping them as three artefacts is correct. Merging the SoA into the inventory produces a document that is neither a decision record nor an operating list, and which has to be untangled at the next audit.

The boundary of the management system, stated under clause 4.3. Everything in
the SoA is a decision made relative to it, which is why an exclusion that
contradicts scope fails immediately.

Review it whenever the scope changes, whenever the risk assessment produces a new treatment, and at the annual management review. A SoA carrying last year’s scope is the most common documentation finding in surveillance audits, and it is entirely avoidable.
