entries.title: What GRC roles exist
entries.description: Analyst, manager, lead, head — plus the four specialisations the work splits into. What each seat does daily, what it pays attention to, and where each one goes next.
sources: ISACA, State of Cybersecurity, workforce sections, 2025

sections.text: What each seat is measured on

blocks.html:
The titles vary more than the work does. Every seat in this field is
accountable for one or more of the four artefacts, and the useful way to read a
job advert is to work out which.

Salary bands are deliberately omitted here: they move, they are regional, and a number in a reference work goes stale in a way the rest of an entry does not. What follows is what each seat actually does.

items.html: The entry seat. Runs the register day to day, chases evidence, completes customer questionnaires, keeps the policy set current. Most of the week is writing things down so somebody else can act on them.
Owns a framework end to end and the audit relationship that goes with it. First seat with a budget conversation and the first with a genuine right to say no.
Owns the register, the appetite statement and the committee reporting. Divergence point: this seat drifts toward the business, the compliance seat toward the auditors.
Owns the programme and the board narrative. Answers for the function’s opinion rather than its paperwork, and spends more time on resourcing than on controls.

blocks.html:
Third-party risk. The first split in almost every organisation, because the volume of supplier assessments is relentless and unlike the rest of the work.

Privacy. A distinct obligation set with its own regulator, its own artefacts and — where a statutory DPO is required — independence constraints that make it a poor fit for a general compliance seat.

Technology / product compliance. Sits closest to engineering. Owns the controls that live in the pipeline, and needs enough fluency to challenge an architecture decision.

Financial controls / SOX. A different lineage entirely, closer to internal audit and the finance function, with its own qualification path.

blocks.text: What each seat is measured on

blocks.html:
Not by controls implemented, in any function worth working in. Analysts are measured on whether the artefacts are current and legible. Managers on whether audits produce surprises. Heads on whether the board’s picture of risk matches the organisation’s actual position.

An interview question worth asking in the other direction: how do you know this function is working? An answer in terms of coverage percentages describes a function that reports on itself. An answer in terms of decisions made and surprises avoided describes one that is used.

The specialist functions providing expertise, challenge and monitoring to the
first line. Almost every GRC seat sits here.

Sideways more often than up, and that is normal. Risk to privacy, compliance to internal audit, GRC to security architecture, and — increasingly — GRC into product, because the person who understands the obligations understands what the product has to do.

The route out that surprises people is into consulting, where the breadth of a generalist seat is worth more than the depth of a specialist one.

entries.title: Breaking into GRC
entries.description: The field hires from IT support, audit, project delivery and law more often than from graduate schemes. What transfers, what has to be learned, and the one artefact that beats a certificate in an interview.
sources: ISACA, CRISC and CISA job practice areas, 2025

sections.text: What each route brings, and what it lacks
The thing that beats a certificate
The gap that actually blocks people

blocks.html:
Almost nobody starts here. The field hires from IT support, internal audit,
project delivery and law, and each route arrives with most of one half of the
job already done.
Knowing which half you already have is the difference between a targeted application and a scattergun one.

blocks.text: What each route brings, and what it lacks

items.html: Brings the ability to read a system you did not build and write down what happened. Lacks the evidence habit — what makes a screenshot admissible, why a date matters, what the auditor asks next.
Brings sampling, testing and the discipline of writing findings that survive challenge. Lacks the design side: this seat has never had to build the control it has spent years testing.
Brings tracking, chasing and getting a dozen people to a date. Lacks the domain — which obligations exist and why they bind.
Brings obligation reading and precision about sources. Lacks the technical literacy to challenge an engineer’s answer without accepting it whole.

blocks.text: The thing that beats a certificate

blocks.html:
One artefact you built, that you can walk somebody through end to end.

A risk you assessed: how it was raised, how you scored it and against what scale, who owned it, what treatment was chosen, who approved it, what evidence closed it. Ten minutes, specific, with the parts that went wrong included.

A candidate who can do that outperforms one with three certificates and nothing to describe, every time, because the interviewer’s actual question is whether you have handled a real artefact or only read about them.

If your current job has none, build one. Assess a risk in your own team’s work, properly, with a documented scale. It is a real artefact even if the organisation never asked for it.

They help with the screening filter and they do not close the interview.

CISA is the most widely recognised in audit-adjacent roles and does not assume a technical background. ISO 27001 Lead Implementer teaches the management-system vocabulary faster than anything else. Sequencing matters more than choice: a certificate taken before you have handled an artefact teaches you vocabulary with nothing to attach it to, and it fades.

blocks.text: The gap that actually blocks people

blocks.html:
Not technical depth. The evidence habit — understanding that the job is not doing the thing but being able to show, months later, to somebody who was not there, that the thing was done.

It is learnable in months and it is the thing hiring managers are listening for. Candidates who talk about what they did are common; candidates who talk about what they kept are not.

entries.title: Interview questions, and how to answer them
entries.description: The eight questions that come up in almost every GRC interview, what each one is really testing, and the shape of an answer that lands.

blocks.html:
Every one of these questions has a textbook answer and a real answer. The
textbook answer gets you to the next question; the real answer gets you the job.

What interviewers are testing, almost without exception, is whether you have held the artefact or only read about it. Answers that name a specific instance do that; answers that recite a definition do not.

items.q: What is the difference between GRC and internal audit?
items.html:
The accountability line, not the task list. “GRC reports to management and owns the outcome; internal audit reports to the audit committee and owns the opinion.” Everything about tools and frameworks follows from it.

The follow-up is usually about independence, and the answer they are listening for is that it is structural rather than personal — an auditor who helped fix the gap has lost the opinion they were hired to give, however honest they are. See 1.4.

items.q: Appetite or tolerance — what is the difference?
items.html:
Appetite is how much risk the organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives, set annually by the board, usually by category. Tolerance is the acceptable variation around one specific objective, and it is a number you can cross.

The good answer adds when the distinction bites: at the moment somebody has to decide whether a specific risk gets treated or accepted. See 3.2.

items.q: Walk me through a risk you assessed.
items.html:
The one that matters. Pick a real one, and include what went wrong.

How it was raised. How you scored it, against what documented scale. Who owned it — a person. What treatment was chosen and who had the authority to approve it. What evidence closed it. Then the honest part: what you would do differently, which is where the interview stops being a test.

items.q: How do you handle a control owner who will not give you evidence?
items.html:
They are testing whether you escalate straight away, which is the wrong answer.

Find out why first — usually the request is ambiguous, the system cannot produce what you asked for, or they do not know they own the control. Then make the request specific and easy. Escalation is the third move, not the first, and when it comes it goes with a record of the two attempts before it.

items.q: ISO 27001 or SOC 2?
items.html:
Answer with a question: who is asking for it. North American technology buyers ask for SOC 2; European and enterprise procurement asks for ISO. If both, sequence rather than choose.

Candidates who answer with a preference are describing a document they have read. Candidates who answer with the buyer are describing work they have done. See 5.1.

items.q: Is GRC a technical job?
items.html:
No, but it is a literate one. You need to read a system diagram and challenge an engineer’s answer; you do not need to configure the system.

Worth adding the failure mode, because it shows self-awareness: the risk is not being insufficiently technical, it is accepting an answer you did not understand because asking again felt awkward.

items.q: How would you build a programme from nothing?
items.html:
Register first, even a rough one, because the argument about the scale is easier with real entries in front of it. Then the policy set, then the control inventory with its mapping, then the evidence habit.

Starting with policy is the intuitive answer and the slow one — you end up writing rules for risks you have not established you carry. Saying so demonstrates you have thought about order rather than listing artefacts.

items.q: Where do you see the function failing?
items.html:
An invitation, and most candidates waste it on something generic about tone at the top.

Better: name a failure mode you have seen. Registers where nothing has moved in two quarters. Treatment columns full of “monitor”. Evidence collected in the four weeks before fieldwork. Each of those is specific, checkable, and shows you know what a working function looks like because you know what a broken one looks like.

blocks.html:
Two questions worth more than a dozen polite ones.

How do you know this function is working? Coverage percentages describe a function that reports on itself; decisions made and surprises avoided describe one that is used.

What was the last finding you disagreed with, and what happened? The answer tells you whether the function has standing, or whether it writes what it is asked to write.

entries.description: ISO 27001, CISA, CISM, CRISC, CISSP, SANS and GRC courses side by side — what each certifies, who it suits, and why a beginner needs breadth before a badge.
sources: ISACA, CISA / CISM / CRISC certification requirements, 2025
(ISC)² CISSP experience, endorsement and CBK domains, 2024
GIAC certification catalogue and eligibility, SANS Institute, 2025
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — lead implementer / auditor grades are provider schemes (PECB, BSI and others)

sections.text: Sequencing, which matters more than choice

blocks.html:
No single GRC certification suits every role. The right one depends on the seat
you are aiming at, how much experience you already have, and whether your
immediate need is broad grounding or specialist evidence — and most of the
respected credentials are narrower than their reputation suggests.

Almost all of the well-known certifications qualify a slice of the work rather than GRC as a whole — an audit exam, a risk exam, a management exam, a security generalist’s exam, a single standard. For someone already in a seat, that focus is the point. For someone entering the field it is the trap: a specialist credential bought before there is any context to attach it to teaches vocabulary with nothing behind it.

The options a newcomer actually weighs, described by what each one is rather than how it markets itself. The last column is the experience needed to hold the credential, not to sit the exam.

Path What it certifies Who it suits Breadth Experience to be certified
GRC foundation course A taught grounding in how the function works Someone entering GRC from any route Broad — the function end to end (varies by provider) None
ISO 27001 Lead Implementer / Auditor Competence to implement or audit one standard Someone standing up or auditing an ISMS Narrow — a single standard Scheme-dependent: provisional grades none, full lead grades several years
ISACA CISA Information systems audit, governance and control Auditors and audit-adjacent roles Specialised — the audit seat Five years in IS audit, control or security; up to three waivable
ISACA CRISC IT risk identification and control Risk-register and control practitioners Specialised — the risk seat Three years across two or more of four domains; no waivers
ISACA CISM Information security management Practitioners moving into a security-management role Specialised — the management seat Five years in information security, three of them in security management
ISC2 CISSP Broad security across eight domains Security generalists and leads Broad in security, thin on GRC Five years across two or more of the eight domains; one year waivable
SANS / GIAC Hands-on technical skill in a chosen domain Practitioners doing the technical work Deep and domain-specific; some management and audit tracks too GIAC exams: none formal

The credential exams — CISA, CRISC, CISM and CISSP — can each be sat before that experience is complete, but the certification itself waits on it. Read the last column as a destination, not a starting line.

Two patterns. First, every credential in the table is either specialised — the audit seat, the risk seat, the management seat, one standard, one technical domain — or, in CISSP’s case, broad across security engineering rather than across governance, risk and compliance. None of them is a general grounding in the GRC function itself.

Second, all of them assume experience a newcomer does not yet have. They are things you work toward from inside a seat, while the experience accrues, not things you enter the field holding.

What a person entering GRC needs first is the opposite shape: a working map of the whole function — the four artefacts, how a register is scored, what an auditor asks for — that assumes nothing and is tied to no single standard or vendor. With a target seat already in view, the matching credential can come first; without one, the grounding comes first, because a specialist exam taken with no context to attach it to does not stick.

blocks.text: Sequencing, which matters more than choice

blocks.html:
The order tends to beat the pick. If you already know the seat you are heading for, the matching credential is a reasonable first move: CISA for audit, CRISC for an IT-risk role, CISM once you are in a security-management role, an ISO lead course if your first job is standing up an ISMS. If you do not, start with the general grounding and one real artefact you have handled — the walk-through in 6.1 — then choose.

Certifications do most of their work at the screening stage, where a recognised acronym gets a CV read; they do less in the interview, where a specific artefact you can walk through tends to carry more weight than a badge. How that balance falls is employer-dependent, but it is worth knowing which investment does which job.

items.q: What is the best GRC certification?
items.html: There is no single best one, because the certifications answer different questions. CISA is the credential most often asked for in audit-facing roles, CRISC maps to the risk seat, CISM to a security-management role, and CISSP to broad security leadership. For someone entering GRC without a seat in mind, breadth matters more than any one exam: a grounding in the whole function, taken before the specialist badge, is what makes the badge worth having.

items.q: Which GRC certification should I get first?
items.html: If you know the role you are targeting, the credential that matches it. If you do not, usually none first — start with a broad grounding in how the function works and one real artefact you have handled, then choose the certification that fits the seat you are moving toward. A specialist exam taken with no context is hard to retain.

items.q: Is CISA worth it for GRC?
items.html: For audit-adjacent GRC roles it is among the most commonly requested credentials, and it sets no formal education or technical-role prerequisite. Note the experience requirement: five years of IS audit, control or security work, with up to three years of permitted substitutions. You can sit the exam earlier; certification waits on the experience.

items.q: Is CISSP a GRC certification?
items.html: No. CISSP is a broad information-security certification across eight domains. One of them — security and risk management — covers governance, risk and compliance directly, but the certification as a whole is security engineering and leadership rather than GRC operational work, and it does not centre on the artefacts a GRC seat produces.

items.q: Do I need a certification to get into GRC?
items.html: No. A certification helps pass the CV screen; it does not close an interview. A candidate who can walk through one risk they assessed — how it was scored, who owned it, what evidence closed it — tends to outperform one with certificates and nothing to describe. Build the artefact either way.

entries.title: How a GRC career progresses
entries.description: Analyst to manager to head is a change in what you own, not a bigger version of the same job. What earns each move, how long it takes, and where people stall.
keywords: how to get promoted in GRC
sources: ISACA, State of Cybersecurity, workforce sections, 2025

blocks.html:
Progression in GRC is not doing more of the analyst job faster. Each move up
hands you a different thing to own — first a framework, then a programme, then
the board’s picture of risk — and the people who stall are usually the ones
doing the lower job extremely well.
The ladder has three real rungs, whatever the titles in between suggest. What separates them is not time served but what you can be handed without supervision.

Analyst to manager. The analyst runs the register, chases evidence and completes questionnaires — work measured on whether the artefacts are current and legible. The manager owns a framework end to end and the audit relationship that comes with it. The step is the first time you carry a right to say no: to a control owner, to a timeline, to a scope. Nobody hands that over because you processed questionnaires quickly; they hand it over once you have shown judgement about which risks matter and which findings are worth the fight.

Manager to head. The manager answers for a framework; the head answers for the programme and the narrative the board hears. The work shifts from controls to resourcing, from the audit to the story of the function’s risk position. This is the move where technical fluency stops being the constraint and political literacy starts — the head who cannot get a budget conversation to land is limited regardless of how well they understand the controls.

The sideways move. More common than either, and not a demotion. Risk to privacy, compliance to internal audit, GRC to security architecture or into product. Each rebuilds depth in a new domain on top of the general grounding, and a person with two domains behind them is worth more than one with a single deep specialisation, particularly on the route into consulting.

Not certifications, and not tenure. The signal is the same at every rung: an artefact you owned and a decision you made that turned out to be right.

The analyst earns the manager seat by showing judgement — pushing back on a finding, spotting a risk before it was raised, running a piece of the framework without being told the next step. The manager earns the head seat by owning an outcome the board saw: an audit that produced no surprises, a risk position that matched reality when it was tested. Each move is granted on evidence of the next job, done early, not on mastery of the current one.

The permanent analyst is the common one: someone excellent at the mechanics who never develops the judgement calls that the next seat is made of. The mechanics are visible and rewarded, so it is comfortable to stay, and the register keeps running. The way out is to start making the calls before you are asked to — form a view on which risks matter, argue a finding, own a decision — because the seat is granted to people already doing its work, not promised to people who have earned a turn.

The second plateau is the specialist who went deep too early, built a career on one framework, and finds the head-of-function role wants breadth they traded away. Depth is valuable and it is also a ceiling if it is the only thing you have.

items.q: How long does it take to go from analyst to manager?
items.html: There is no fixed number, because the move is granted on demonstrated judgement rather than years served. Some make it inside two years by owning real decisions early; others run the register competently for longer without ever showing the judgement the next seat requires. Time is a weak predictor; what you have owned is a strong one.

items.q: Do I need a certification to get promoted in GRC?
items.html: Rarely for the move itself. Certifications help you get hired and pass CV screens; promotion turns on whether you have shown you can do the next job. A certification that matches your target seat — CISM heading into management, CRISC into a risk role — can support the case, but it does not make it. See 6.3.

items.q: Is GRC manager a technical role?
items.html: Usually it shifts away from hands-on work rather than toward it: the job is owning a framework, the audit relationship and a set of decisions, and the constraint is judgement more than technical depth. How much fluency it needs still varies by organisation and domain — a manager over cloud or product controls reads more architecture than one over policy and third-party risk. You need enough to challenge an engineer’s answer either way.

entries.title: A day in the life of a GRC analyst
entries.description: What a GRC analyst does all week — questionnaires, evidence chasing, register updates and one hard conversation. How technical it is depends on the seat.
keywords: day in the life GRC analyst
what does a GRC analyst do
sources: ISACA, State of Cybersecurity, workforce sections, 2025

blocks.html:
Most of a GRC analyst’s week is turning other people’s work into a record
somebody can act on months later, when the person who did the work is not in the
room. It is writing-heavy, meeting-heavy and deadline-driven, and for a typical
compliance-facing seat far less of it is hands-on technical than people expect.

The rhythm is a steady cadence of recurring work with periodic spikes around audits and questionnaires, not a queue of tickets. Knowing which kind of work is in front of you is most of managing the week.
Some things come round on a cycle whether or not anything has happened.

items.html: Keeping risk entries current — chasing owners for updates, moving review dates, flagging anything that has drifted past its date. The register is only as trustworthy as its most stale row.

Collecting the artefacts that show a control operated — an access review, a change record, a backup test — and filing them so they are legible to someone who was not there. The habit, not the collection, is the skill.
Nudging policies through their review dates, tracking exceptions and waivers, keeping the set consistent when one document changes.
The routine control checks that recur monthly or quarterly, where the work is noticing the exception in a list that is mostly fine.

blocks.html:
Then there is the work that arrives, usually with a date attached.

A security questionnaire from a prospect’s procurement team, which has to be answered accurately and fast because a deal is waiting on it. An audit window, where weeks of collected evidence get assembled, gaps get closed under time pressure, and the analyst is the person who knows where everything is. A new obligation — a contract clause, a regulation, a customer requirement — that has to be mapped to a control before anyone can say whether it is met.

The triggered work is where the recurring work pays off: an analyst who kept the evidence current all quarter has a calm audit week, and one who did not has a bad one.

Nearly every week contains a version of the same conversation: a control owner who has not produced what you asked for. The skill is not escalation — it is finding out why first (usually the request was ambiguous or the system cannot produce it), making the ask specific and easy, and keeping a record. Most of the job’s friction lives in this exchange, and handling it well is what separates a useful analyst from an irritating one.

Three things, consistently. It is writing-heavy — the output is documents and records, not configurations. For a typical compliance-facing seat it is not hands-on technical; you read systems and challenge answers rather than build them, though analysts embedded with a cloud, identity or data team do need that depth. And it is deadline-driven in bursts rather than uniformly busy, with quiet cadence weeks and intense audit weeks. The tools are a GRC platform, a spreadsheet and a ticketing system — the platform matters less than the discipline behind what goes into it.

items.q: Is GRC work boring?
items.html: It is administrative in stretches and it is not a coding job, so people expecting constant technical problem-solving find the cadence work slow. What keeps it engaging for the people who stay is the judgement — deciding which risks matter, handling the control-owner conversation, seeing the whole organisation’s exposure in a way few other seats do.

items.q: What does a GRC analyst do all day?
items.html: Keeps the register current, collects and files evidence, answers security questionnaires, runs recurring control checks, and chases the people whose work those records depend on. Most of the day is turning other people’s activity into a record that will hold up later.

items.q: How technical is a GRC analyst role?
items.html: It depends on the seat. A typical compliance-facing analyst needs to be literate rather than hands-on: read a system diagram, understand what a control does, and challenge an engineer’s answer without accepting it whole, without configuring the system or writing code. An analyst embedded with a cloud or platform team may need real technical depth — cloud IAM, logging, scripting. See 6.0 for how that changes across the seats.

pages.editorial_policy:
Editorial policy

How entries are written, who reviews them, and what gets corrected.

1WHO WRITES THIS

Entries are written by practitioners who have done the work being described — run the register, sat the audit, written the policy that was later tested. Every entry names its editor and the credential they hold. An entry with no named editor is not published.

2REVIEW CYCLE

Each entry carries a review date and an edition number. Entries are reviewed quarterly, and sooner when a source standard is revised. The review date is the date a human read the entry against its sources, not the date a file changed.

3SOURCES
